_summary: Deterministic phishing-link heuristics for the AI Inbox reader. Consumed by MailLinkAssessor.swift. Authoritative source of truth — the Swift binary carries only clamped _fallback_only defaults, because threat lists go stale in days and shipped users cannot recompile.
_redirectors_note: Link wrappers that carry the real destination inside a parameter. `encoding` says how to read it: 'plain' = percent-decoded parameter value. Anything else is NOT decoded in v1 — the assessor reports redirectorNotDecoded and refuses to guess a destination rather than showing a garbled one. Adding a decoder is a Swift change; adding a wrapper that uses an existing decoder is content-only.
_generic_note: Applied to ANY host when a parameter holds something that parses as an absolute http(s) URL. Catches the long tail of marketing redirectors without naming them.
_tld_note: Risk tiers, not a blocklist. A risky TLD alone is CAUTION, never DANGER — plenty of legitimate mail uses .link and .live. It escalates when it co-occurs with another signal.
_impersonation_note: Hosts whose NAME appearing anywhere other than the authority position is a deception signal — the 'https://mail.google.com/https://evil.icu/' shape. Naming these is how impersonation is detected; it is not branding content.
_credential_note: Path/query tokens that mean 'this page wants your identity'. Harmless alone; they set the stakes when the host is already suspect.
_knownBad_note: Seeded from a real 2026-09-23 phish reported by the owner. This list is a courtesy, not the mechanism — the heuristics above must catch an unlisted domain of the same shape, and the unit test asserts exactly that by scoring this URL with the list emptied.
_attachment_note: Extensions that execute or can carry a macro/loader. Advisory only — the reader never blocks a download, it labels it.
_scoring_note: Weights sum to a score; the score picks a tier. Tunable without a rebuild — that is the point of putting it here. Any single reason with weight >= dangerAt reaches DANGER on its own.
